**H1 explains only part of it. The 2022-2025 markdown rise ($4,059,115 on stock lines) is mostly the mixed-refrigerant 2023 cohort, which Hartwell keeps stocking and sells below cost. A real R-410A clearance began in 2025, and its cost arrives mainly in 2026**

Hartwell keeps restocking 264 SKUs from the 2015 and 2023 discontinued groups. An automatic markdown tied to their discontinued_on date pushes the stock-line price below an unchanged buy cost, so these lines lost $2,789,637 in 2025. Confidence is high. The next step is for purchasing and pricing to review each of the 264 SKUs and either stop replenishment or correct discontinued_on, and to count only stock lines in markdown reporting. The R-410A clearance is separate and still growing: re-run q232 and q239 monthly in 2026, since the 3,442 units on hand would carry $2,544,097 of markdown at the 42% cap.

**H3 is not supported as stated. R-410A stock is at a ten-year low, and its 2025 below-cost sales are one case of a company-wide pattern: once any equipment SKU passes its discontinued_on date, stock-fulfilled lines sell below cost and keep getting replenished. Losses on those stock lines averaged $1,689,105.48 a year over 2023-2025**

Across all equipment, stock lines sold after a SKU's discontinued_on date lost $1,689,105.48 a year on average over 2023-2025. Special-order and transfer lines of the same SKUs held about 1.20x cost, and stock buying of discontinued SKUs kept rising, to 10,001 units in 2025. Confidence is medium, and not all of the loss is avoidable, because demand at full price is unobserved. The next step is to pull the stock-line pricing setup and the reorder parameters for discontinued SKUs, starting with the 44 R-410A SKUs discontinued 2015-01-01. The product manager should also confirm whether those dates are correct. This finding and the one above measure overlapping stock-line losses, so their dollars should not be added together.

**H2 only partly holds: outside markdowns, price-to-list fell about 1 point because low-discount accounts in every cohort stop buying faster, not because accounts were repriced or new accounts signed at bigger discounts. That is $1.43M a year of price erosion on 2025 volume, not a sum retention would recover.**

Outside markdowns, price-to-list fell from 0.8442 in 2016 to 0.8343 in 2025. The cause is that accounts with discounts under 10% stop ordering faster, and this holds in every size group, trade and branch. On 2025 volume that amounts to $1,428,556.44 of price erosion. Confidence is medium. Retention would not win this money back; the larger cost is probably lost volume, since non-markdown list value fell by $9,502,085.00. The next step is to list lapsed under-10% accounts with their last order day, branch and account-manager rep_id, so account managers can ask why each one stopped. IT should also be asked whether discount_pct changes are logged.

What did not hold up: the 2022-2025 markdown rise is not an R-410A clearance, and Hartwell is not overstocked on R-410A. Year-end 2025 R-410A stock of 5,601 units was the lowest of 2016-2025. The below-cost selling follows the discontinued flag, not the refrigerant type. The $6,620,818 of recorded 2025 markdown on special and transfer lines was never actually given, because invoices show full prices. There is no sign that anyone priced lines by hand, favoured customers, repriced existing accounts or signed new accounts at bigger discounts.

What the records can't answer:
- What discontinued_on means to the business, and whether the dates are right.
- Why replenishment keeps buying discontinued SKUs.
- Why the markdown doesn't reach special and transfer lines.
- Whether sales volume would hold at full price.
- How fast the remaining R-410A stock will sell in 2026.
- Why low-discount accounts stop ordering.
- Whether discount_pct ever changed.
- Margin based on historical cost, and any off-bill rebates.

Answering these needs product lifecycle records, vendor end-of-life notices, the pricing-rule configuration, a discount change log and 2026 sales.
